lessons.title: Compute with numbers
lessons.summary: If score starts at 6, what does score <- score * 3 store?
explanation:
For numbers in R, + adds, - subtracts, and * multiplies.

Subtraction takes two numeric operands and returns their difference; multiplication returns their product. Neither expression reassigns its operands.
```r
cat(7 - 2, "\n", sep = "")
cat(3 * 4, "\n", sep = "")
```
It prints:
```text
5
12
```
On the right of an assignment, R computes the expression before changing the name on the left.
score <- score + 2 therefore uses the old score to calculate its replacement.
This lesson uses single numbers. R also supports sequences of values called vectors, whose behavior is a later topic.

```r
score <- 5
score <- score + 2
print(score)
```
Expected result: [1] 7. Follow the instructions in order; this is a worked example, not an in-app execution.

lessons.title: Logical vectors and scalar conditions
lessons.summary: Replace the right operand TRUE with FALSE. What prints?
explanation: c(TRUE,FALSE) is a two-element logical vector. NA can represent an unknown logical value.

& and | operate elementwise. && and || are short-circuit operators for scalar conditions; supplying a vector longer than one is an error in this tested runtime.

The elementwise | combines corresponding logical entries. && and || use scalar logical choices: false on the left decides &&, and true on the left decides || without evaluating the right expression.
```r
cat(c(TRUE, FALSE) | c(FALSE, FALSE), sep = ",")
cat("\n")
cat(FALSE && TRUE, "\n", sep = "")
cat(TRUE || FALSE, "\n", sep = "")
```
It prints:
```text
TRUE,FALSE
FALSE
TRUE
```

if needs one non-missing logical result. A scalar numeric value can be coerced to logical, but explicit comparisons make intent clearer. It does not choose a policy for an entire vector or an unknown value.

lessons.title: Logical indexing with missing values
lessons.summary: Add the explicit !is.na(values) & check to the mask. What prints?

lessons.title: Lists and extraction operators
lessons.summary: Change items[1] to items[[1]]. What type prints?
explanation: list(score=7, topic="stars") stores a number and text as separate components without forcing one common atomic type.
items[1] returns a one-component list. items[[1]] extracts the component itself. That extracted component can be a vector or another complex object.

items$score is convenient for a fixed component name. For programmatically supplied exact names, [[ with an explicit name is clearer than relying on partial matching.

[[ with index 1 and $ with fixed name score both extract the stored component itself here, not a one-component list. Each returns the numeric value 7.
```r

cat(items[[1]], items$score, sep = ",")
```

```text
7,7
```

lessons.title: Spread quantiles and units
lessons.summary: If every value is multiplied by 2, what happens to sd and IQR?
explanation:
sprintf("%.1f", x) formats a number as text with one decimal place; it changes display, not the stored number. sd estimates sample standard deviation using denominator n - 1; its unit matches the observations. var(x) receives numeric observations and returns their sample variance, the square of sample standard deviation, in squared units. quantile receives observations and requested probabilities and returns estimated cut points; R supports several definitions, so type = 7 is explicit here.

Here probs = c(0.25, 0.75) requests the lower and upper quartiles.
```r

cat(sprintf("%.1f", var(x)), "\n", sep = "")
cat(sprintf("%.1f", quantile(x, probs = c(0.25, 0.75), type = 7)), sep = ",")
```

```text
1.0
1.5,2.5
```

lessons.title: Logistic models and link scales

glm with family = binomial() uses the logit link by default for a binary response. A 0/1 vector records failures/successes. The linear predictor is log-odds, log(p / (1 - p)); it is not itself a probability.

```

-1.099
```

lessons.title: Language objects and trusted evaluation
lessons.summary: If context$x becomes 9 before eval, what value results?
explanation:
quote captures an R expression without evaluating it. eval evaluates that expression in a supplied environment; new.env(parent = baseenv()) gives this example a controlled lookup context for a known expression, not a security sandbox.

baseenv() takes no arguments and returns R's base environment, containing base operations such as +. Using it as the new environment's parent controls where missing names are looked up; it does not restrict what arbitrary evaluated code is allowed to do.

The expression here is authored directly as x + 1 and x is explicitly bound. Parsing arbitrary text and evaluating it can run arbitrary R operations; an environment or an allowlist of variable names alone does not make unknown code safe. Prefer a data format and explicit operations for external input.

```r
expression <- quote(x + 1)
context <- new.env(parent = baseenv())
context$x <- 4
cat(eval(expression, envir = context), "\n", sep = "")

```

explanation:
sessionInfo records the R version, platform and loaded package information. RNGkind describes random-generator configuration; options can also affect behavior and formatting. Saving metadata helps explain a run but does not by itself recreate dependencies, input data or operating-system behavior.

RNGkind() with no arguments returns the current generator, normal-generation and sampling algorithm names without changing them. This is the configuration observed in the tested R 4.5.0 fresh session, not a promise that every session has the same settings.
```r
cat(RNGkind(), sep = " | ")
```
It prints:
```text
Mersenne-Twister | Inversion | Rejection
```

options returns prior values for changed settings, so a function can register on.exit(options(old), add = TRUE). This keeps local formatting from leaking into later analysis. Rscript --vanilla avoids startup files and workspace restoration, but still needs explicit data, package versions and seed policy.

getOption("digits") receives an option name and returns its current value. In the example it reads 3 inside show_value, then reads the restored value after on.exit has run. It does not change the option.

  on.exit(options(old), add = TRUE)
  cat(getOption("digits"), "\n", sep = "")
}
before <- getOption("digits")
show_value()
cat(identical(before, getOption("digits")), "\n", sep = "")

lessons.title: A bounded data-analysis pipeline
lessons.summary: If the first value becomes 65, what is retained and summarized?
explanation:
A bounded pipeline checks type, missingness and domain before summarizing. Here input is a finite real-valued numeric vector; is.finite excludes NA, NaN and infinities, and the accepted range is 1..60 minutes. head(valid, 3) caps the number of retained valid observations.

For ordinary vectors, is.numeric(input) returns TRUE for integer or double values and FALSE for complex values and factors. It does not check finiteness or the allowed minutes range; the separate finite-value and range checks are still needed.

The retained count and arithmetic mean describe only accepted observations in this synthetic input. They do not establish a population mean, causality or real-world validity. Real analysis also needs units, provenance, input-size limits and an explicit exclusion policy; silently dropping data can bias conclusions.
